newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong to avoid over-regulation of banks - Tsang.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong to avoid over-regulation of banks - Tsang.

text.p: Hong Kong will remain vigilant to avoid over-regulation of the banking industry, Financial Secretary Donald Tsang said on Thursday.

"An effective supervisory system was essential to maintain banking stability but ... we cannot simply continue to pile on more and more regulation," Tsang told the Hong Kong Association of Banks' half-yearly dinner.

"Regulation does impose a cost on financial intermediation which is ultimately passed on to the consumer. The regulatory burden placed on banks must therefore be in proportion to the likely benefits."

Speculation has been widespread that the Hong Kong Monetary Authority, the de facto central bank under Tsang's ultimate authority, would introduce tougher property lending restrictions in response to concern about Hong Kong banks' asset quality.
Banks' property exposure has been rising fast as property prices have soared.

But Tsang told the bankers' group that wherever possible, the government hoped to rely on internal risk management exercised by banks themselves, backed by the external discipline imposed by the market and by supervisors.

Tsang also confirmed the government's prior forecast of 5.5-percent growth in gross domestic product this year, and said first quarter growth slightly above six percent would be good for the banking sector, improving loan demand and asset quality.
This strong position bodes well for banks as they confront an era of change, he said.
"At this time of radical change, it is important that banks should be able to rely on government for a solid bedrock of policy and regulation," Tsang said.
"This is what we have tried to provide in the past in Hong Kong, and we shall continue to do so in the future."
But Tsang did not directly refer to the rapid approach of Hong Kong's return to Chinese sovereignty on July 1, instead focusing on globalisation of markets.
Greater market interdependence was heightening systemic risk and the volatility of capital flows, but it was also increasing opportunities, he said.

Deflecting recent criticism of foreign banks, who entered Hong Kong's property boom late but aggressively, Tsang said their willingness to take on long-term Hong Kong dollar residential mortgage loans "is a practical demonstration of confidence in the future of Hong Kong".
But he conceded that greater competition might increase risk by persuading local banks to take on higher-margin, more risky business even while it reduces costs for consumers.

"It is thus important, at a time of rapid change in the business and competitive environment for banks, that there should be stability and continuity in the broader political, legal and regulatory framework within which they operate," he said.

The key elements of an appropriate framework include stable constitutional arrangements, sound and sustainable macroeconomic policies, a well-developed public infrastrcuture, effective market discipline and effective banking supervision.
